q: Why do the reproduced per-model L2 test errors sit systematically 0.07–0.32 pp above the paper's Table 3 numbers, all 5 with the same positive sign? Is this an artifact of re-fitting the missing x/up normalizers from test rather than train, of torch/CUDA-version drift, or of GPU-determinism (RTX 2080 Ti → A100)?
basis: Observed pattern: 5-for-5 positive bias, ~0.1–0.3 pp, with the ensemble also biased +0.13 pp. That is a systematic-not-random signature. The paper's checkpoints ship only y_normalizer, not x_normalizer or up_normalizer, so we had to reconstruct the latter two from the test-set stats — a plausible root cause of the bias.
next_steps: Finish the 2.1 GB train_data_norm.pkl download (~30 min at HF's throttled rate), refit x_normalizer + up_normalizer from the training set exactly as the paper's MIODataset pipeline does, and rerun the full 1,126-sample inference. If the bias vanishes to Δ<0.1pp, the checkpoint-metadata gap is confirmed as the root cause and should be reported to the authors as a metadata bug (their checkpoint save should include all three normalizers, not just y). Also run a torch-2.x + Ampere-TF32-off matrix to isolate version/hw contributions.

q: How does the neural operator's rel-L2 error grow across the 6 output timesteps? Table 3's single scalar is the mean-over-timesteps rel-L2, hiding whether autoregressive-style errors compound as t → +6·30s = +3 min, or whether the model has learned to smooth them out.
basis: The WeightedLpRelLoss `component='all'` code path in learning/data_utils.py computes 6 per-timestep rel-L2 values then averages. The multi-step MPC in Sec. 5.3 rolls out 10 x 6 = 60 output timesteps by feeding predictions back as history, so per-step error growth directly bounds the achievable control horizon before the surrogate has to be reset to the true state.
next_steps: Modify run_bear_inference.py to keep per-timestep rel-L2 tensors instead of averaging, produce a 6-column report (t+30s, +60s, …, +3min) per model + ensemble, and fit a growth curve. Cross-check by running the paper's own control notebook one step at a time with our checkpoints — if per-timestep error is ~monotonic and slow, the 30-min rollout is safe; if it explodes past t+2min, the paper's Fig. 6 result may depend on lucky initial conditions or need occasional CFD resets.

q: Does the ensemble's ~1 pp advantage over the best individual model persist on the hardest-to-predict test samples (e.g., the top-5% by any-single-model L2), or does the ensemble mostly average away noise on easy cases while adding no value on tail cases?
basis: Overall reproduction: ensemble 11.03 % vs best individual (Model 2) 12.04 %. That's a real 8 % relative improvement, but the paper doesn't report tail statistics — and the pathological building-control failure mode is a rare high-occupancy transient where a single model over-predicts CO2 concentration and the controller responds by over-ventilating. Ensemble value on that tail is what actually matters operationally.
next_steps: Sort the 1,126 test-sample rel-L2 residuals per model, take the union of each model's worst-100 samples, and score ensemble vs best-individual on that tail set specifically. Also plot pairwise-disagreement (max_i,j ||mu_i - mu_j||_2 across the 5 models) vs actual error; the paper's Eq. 7b defines a predictive variance sigma_C^2 that should correlate with true error — this is a testable calibration claim not made in the paper.

q: The 250,000x speedup (Table 5) compares a single 6-step NN forward against a single 6-step CFD transient. In the paper's Sec. 5.3 60-step MPC rollout, the NN is called recursively 10 times. What is the amortized wall-clock speedup once the NN's accumulated drift forces occasional CFD 'anchor' steps or once the controller does gradient-based inner optimization (which the paper's controller.solver_grad does, ~100 gradient steps per outer control step)?
basis: controller.py:venti_controler.solver_grad uses 100 Adam iterations against the frozen NN ensemble per outer step. That's 100 forward+backward passes per one 3-min control decision. At 4.5 ms/forward that is ~0.9 s per outer step * 60 = 54 s per 30-min episode, vs. 3.5 h if CFD were in the loop. So the *practically usable* speedup is closer to 3.5 * 3600 / 54 = 233x, not 250,000x. The paper's headline number is the raw ratio, not the amortized-control ratio.
next_steps: Time the full paper's control_optimization.ipynb rollout on the released checkpoints and compare against a synthetic 'CFD-in-loop' timing (3.5 h/case per paper Table 5). Report both raw-forward and amortized-MPC speedups explicitly. This distinction matters because 233x is still enormous — real-time-viable — but the 250,000x number can mislead readers into thinking the surrogate is essentially free.

q: The reproduction confirms the paper's learning-half claims but does not test its control-half claims (Table 4, Fig. 6, 12–56 % energy savings). What is the minimum-cost path to independently reproduce ONE control-strategy row of Table 4 without paying for ANSYS Fluent — e.g., replacing Fluent with an open-source CFD (OpenFOAM 2312 with a comparable k-omega-SST species-transport setup) trained on the same released 300 transient cases?
basis: The BEAR-CFD dataset is CC-BY-4.0, so a re-simulation with OpenFOAM on the same classroom geometry would produce a directly-comparable 'ground truth' for one Case. The paper's controller code is Python + PyTorch, no Fluent binding — Fluent only enters at the 'ground truth' evaluation step. OpenFOAM 2312 has k-omega-SST + species transport, is free, and runs on Argonne CELS boxes.
next_steps: (1) Take one of the 300 released .cas.h5 files, extract geometry + boundary conditions with pyfluent (also released tool but the .cas file itself is Fluent-format), or rebuild the classroom mesh from the paper description (19x13x3.5 m, 18 inlets 0.1349x0.3048 m, 2 outlets, ~0.245M tets). (2) Solve one 30-min transient case in OpenFOAM at 10-s time steps. (3) Compare O(1%) CFD-to-CFD reproducibility. (4) If step 3 passes, wire the OpenFOAM sim as the ground-truth in the paper's control loop and reproduce one row of Table 4. This is roughly 1–2 weeks of a domain-expert engineer's time — worth doing if the ML-claim replication (this document) triggers demand for full end-to-end validation.
